does-a-cdn-cut-s3-egress.html.text:
← Cloud egress cost calculator

Does a CDN still cut S3 egress?

Teams search for “CloudFront vs S3 egress” because a cheaper CDN gigabyte looks like a win. The download still leaves a bill. Every user byte pays CDN egress. Bytes that miss the cache also pay origin fetch from the object store to the CDN. Storage is the same on both paths, so this page leaves it off.

On the default 100 GB month — $0.09 origin, $0.085 CDN, 80% hits — origin-only is $9.00. The CDN path is $8.50 of CDN egress plus $1.80 of miss-fetch, $10.30. Origin-only is $1.30 cheaper. The CDN path matches origin-only around 94.4% hits. At 95% hits the CDN path is $8.95, five cents cheaper. Paste the rates on your current price sheet. This page does not fetch provider prices.

Path CDN / origin egress Origin fetch Request fees Monthly total

Complementary to the two-provider monthly comparison (which object store) and replica vs cross-region pull (a second copy versus pulling the same bytes again) and infrequent access vs standard (retrieve fees after a class change). This page is only the internet transfer path in front of one store. The calculator is arithmetic, not advice. It does not claim a cache will hit at the rate you typed.

Common questions

Does a CDN cut S3 egress?

Not always. Every user download still pays CDN egress. Cache misses also pay origin fetch for the bytes that leave the origin toward the CDN. On a 100 GB month at $0.09 origin and $0.085 CDN, 80% hits bill $10.30 on the CDN path versus $9.00 origin-only. The CDN path matches origin-only around 94.4% hits. Paste your quoted rates; this page does not fetch provider prices.

What hit rate makes a CDN cheaper than origin egress?

The hit-rate floor is the cache-hit percentage where both paths bill the same. Below that floor, origin-only is cheaper on these rates. The page solves that volume from the rates you enter. It does not recommend turning a CDN on or off.

does-a-replica-beat-cross-region-pull.ht.text:
← Cloud egress cost calculator

Does a replica still beat a cross-region pull?

Teams search for “S3 cross-region replication cost” after a job in another region re-reads the same bucket every month. Keep-pulling pays cross-region transfer on every gigabyte that leaves. A replica pays a one-time seed, then storage and any change-sync. Internet/CDN egress is a different page; this one is only region-to-region.

On the default 500 GB dataset — 800 GB pulled a month at $0.02/GB, replica storage $0.023/GB-month, 20 GB of monthly changes — keep-pulling is $16.00. The replica path is $11.50 of storage plus $0.40 of change-sync, $11.90, after a $10.00 seed. The replica path is $4.10 cheaper this month. The seed pays back in about 2.4 months. Over 12 months including the seed the replica path is $152.80 versus $192.00, $39.20 cheaper. The paths match at 595 GB of monthly pull. At 400 GB of pull, keep-pulling is $8.00 and the replica path stays $11.90. Paste the rates on your current price sheet. This page does not fetch provider prices.

Path Seed Storage Change-sync Monthly total Horizon total

Complementary to the two-provider monthly comparison (which object store), CDN vs origin (internet downloads), and infrequent access vs standard (retrieve fees after a class change). This page is only a second-region copy versus pulling the same bytes again. The calculator is arithmetic, not advice. It does not claim a replica will stay in sync at the change volume you typed.

Common questions

Does S3 cross-region replication cost less than pulling the data every month?

Only when the monthly pull is large enough to cover replica storage and change-sync. On a 500 GB dataset pulled 800 GB a month at $0.02/GB, keep-pulling is $16.00. A replica at $0.023/GB-month plus 20 GB of monthly changes is $11.90 after a $10.00 seed. The replica path is $4.10 cheaper this month. The seed pays back in about 2.4 months. Over 12 months including the seed the replica path is $39.20 cheaper ($152.80 vs $192.00). The paths match at 595 GB of monthly pull. Paste your quoted rates; this page does not fetch provider prices.

When does keeping the cross-region pull stay cheaper?

When monthly pull volume sits below replica storage plus change-sync, divided by the cross-region rate. On these defaults that floor is 595 GB/month. At 400 GB of pull, keep-pulling is $8.00 and the replica path is $11.90, so keep-pulling is $3.90 cheaper this month. The page solves that volume from the rates you enter. It does not recommend turning replication on or off.

does-infrequent-access-still-beat-standa.text:
← Cloud egress cost calculator

Does infrequent access still beat standard after restore?

Teams search for “S3 infrequent access restore cost” because a cheaper storage gigabyte looks like a win. The read still leaves a bill. Every stored gigabyte pays the class storage rate. Every gigabyte you get back pays a retrieve fee the standard class often bills at $0. Provider A-vs-B and CDN-vs-origin are different pages. This one is only the storage class on one store.

On the default 500 GB stored and 150 GB read back — $0.023 standard, $0.0125 infrequent, $0.04 per retrieved GB — standard class is $11.50. Infrequent is $6.25 of storage plus $6.00 of retrieve, $12.25. Standard is $0.75 cheaper. Infrequent matches standard at 131.3 GB retrieved. At 100 GB retrieved infrequent is $10.25, $1.25 cheaper. Paste the rates on your current price sheet. This page does not fetch provider prices.

Class Storage Retrieve Request fees Monthly total

Complementary to the two-provider monthly comparison (which object store), CDN vs origin (cache hits versus pulling the same bytes), and replica vs cross-region pull (a second copy versus pulling again). This page is only the storage class. The calculator is arithmetic, not advice. It does not claim a restore will stay at the volume you typed, and it does not model minimum storage duration.

Common questions

Does S3 infrequent access still save money after restore fees?

Not always. The infrequent class bills less to store a gigabyte and more to read it back. On the default 500 GB stored and 150 GB retrieved — $0.023 standard, $0.0125 infrequent, $0.04 per retrieved GB — standard is $11.50. Infrequent is $6.25 storage plus $6.00 retrieve, $12.25. Standard is $0.75 cheaper. Infrequent matches standard at 131.3 GB retrieved. Paste your quoted rates; this page does not fetch provider prices.

How much can I restore each month before infrequent access costs more than standard?

The restore-GB ceiling is the monthly retrieve volume where both classes bill the same. Above that volume, standard is cheaper on these rates. The page solves that volume from the rates you enter. It does not recommend changing a storage class.

Common questions

How much does S3 egress cost?

Egress is billed per gigabyte of outbound transfer at the rate on your current price sheet. On the default 500 GB stored, 2 million requests, and 100 GB outbound example, a $0.023 / $0.40 / $0.09 sheet is $21.30 per month. An alternative at $0.006 / $0.36 / $0.00 is $3.72. The $17.58 gap is $210.96 per year. Paste your quoted rates; this page does not fetch provider prices.

Does a cheaper storage rate still win after egress?

Only when outbound transfer is low enough. If cheap storage has a higher egress rate, the page shows the break-even outbound volume. Above that volume the other option is cheaper. The comparison is arithmetic from the rates you enter, not a migration recommendation.

What outbound volume is the break-even point?

The volume where storage-and-request savings and the egress-rate gap cancel out: below it the cheaper-storage, pricier-egress option wins; above it, the other one does. Example: 500 GB stored and 2 million requests at $0.006/GB-month storage, $0.36/million requests, and $0.09/GB egress totals $9.12/month at 60 GB outbound — cheaper than $0.023/$0.40/$0 storage's $12.30. Push outbound to 150 GB and the same cheap-egress sheet totals $17.22, more than the $12.30 alternative. The crossover on this pair is 95.33 GB/month; the page computes it for whatever rates and workload you enter.

Does this include migration cost or contract minimums?

No. The monthly total is storage, request, and egress charges only — it does not add a one-time data-transfer-out fee for the move itself, a minimum monthly commitment your contract may require, or the engineering time to actually migrate. Check your price sheet and contract for those before deciding on this number alone.

vs-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← Cloud Egress Cost Calculator

This calculator vs. estimating egress in a spreadsheet

Storage-and-egress arithmetic looks simple enough to do in one spreadsheet cell: multiply the outbound gigabytes by the per-GB rate on the quote. The arithmetic is not wrong -- the formula is just simpler than the price sheet it is pricing, in two specific ways that both push the estimate higher than the real bill.

StepCommon spreadsheet shortcutWhat this calculator does
The free monthly allowance Bills every outbound gigabyte from the first one, because a flat =volume*rate formula has no cell for "the first N GB are free." Subtracts your entered free-egress allowance before any rate is applied, for both options.
Graduated rate steps Applies one rate to the whole billable volume, when the published sheet is usually "next 10,240 GB at $X, everything beyond at a lower $Y." Walks a pasted multi-band rate sheet the same way the provider bills it, cheaper bands and all.
The break-even outbound volume Requires solving a piecewise crossing between two multi-segment curves by hand for every new pair of quotes. Computes the outbound GB where the two options bill the same, honoring both options' allowances and bands.
Does anything I type get uploaded anywhere? N/A No. The comparison runs entirely in your browser; nothing you enter is sent to a server.

A worked example

Take a workload of 2,000 GB stored, 8 million requests/month, and 15,000 GB of outbound transfer, priced at $0.023/GB storage and $0.40/million requests on both approaches. The only difference is how the egress line is billed:

ApproachEgress lineTotal
Flat spreadsheet formula 15,000 GB × $0.09/GB, no free allowance $1,399.20
This calculator 100 GB free, then 10,240 GB at $0.09 and 4,660 GB at $0.085 $1,366.90

The gap is $32.30/month -- $387.60/year -- on rates that were never typed in wrong, only applied one step more simply than the price sheet actually bills them. Paste the rate sheet you were actually quoted, including any free allowance and graduated bands, and the calculator applies all of it.

Common questions

What does a quick spreadsheet formula usually get wrong about egress?

Two things, both because a single =volume*rate cell is the easiest formula to write, not because the price sheet actually works that way. First, it bills from the first byte, when every major provider gives some GB of outbound transfer free each month before the per-GB rate starts. Second, it applies one flat rate to the whole volume, when the published rate steps down as volume grows -- "the next 10,240 GB at $0.09, everything beyond at $0.085" is how a real sheet reads, not one number for every gigabyte.

How much difference does that actually make?

On a workload of 2,000 GB stored, 8 million requests, and 15,000 GB of outbound transfer a month, a flat $0.09/GB spreadsheet formula totals $1,399.20. The same workload against a sheet with a 100 GB free allowance and a $0.085/GB step past 10,240 billable GB totals $1,366.90 -- $32.30/month, $387.60/year, on rates that were never wrong, only applied more simply than the provider actually bills them.

Can a spreadsheet formula just add the free allowance and the rate steps itself?

Yes, and a careful one often does for a single quote. What it does not do without real effort is the break-even: the outbound volume at which a cheaper-storage, pricier-egress option stops winning against the alternative. That is a piecewise crossing between two multi-segment curves, not a single-cell formula, and re-deriving it by hand for every new pair of rate sheets is exactly the kind of one-off arithmetic this calculator exists to skip.

Does this page publish any provider's actual current rates?

No. The $0.09/$0.085 rate step and the 100 GB free allowance in the worked example above are illustrative figures chosen to show the arithmetic, not a quotation of any provider's published price list. Paste in the rates from your own current quote; this calculator computes from what you enter and fetches nobody's price sheet.

Open the Cloud Egress Cost Calculator to run this on your own rate sheet, or see how it handles a CDN in front of the same store, a cross-region replica, or infrequent-access storage.

vs-aws-pricing-calculator.html.text:
← Cloud Egress Cost Calculator

This calculator vs. the AWS Pricing Calculator

AWS publishes its own free estimation tool, the AWS Pricing Calculator, at calculator.aws, with background and FAQs at aws.amazon.com/aws-cost-management/aws-pricing-calculator/faqs. You pick a service such as S3, a region, a storage class, and expected usage, and it prices that configuration against AWS's own published rate card, either as a one-off workload estimate or a full consolidated bill.

That makes it the right tool for one job: what a specific AWS configuration will cost, on AWS's current published prices. It reads AWS's own price list, so it is authoritative in a way no third-party page, including this one, can be. This site does not publish AWS's current per-GB rates or claim to, and it prices only AWS services -- it has no notion of a non-AWS provider's rate card, because there is no "other cloud" line item to select. If you need a current AWS estimate, that is the tool to open, and this page says so.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What will this exact AWS S3 configuration cost this month, on AWS's current price list? AWS's own Pricing Calculator — it is the live source.
Given the two rate sheets I was actually quoted, which one is cheaper for my workload? This calculator — storage, requests, and egress on one screen, from the numbers you paste in.
At what outbound-transfer volume does the cheaper-storage option stop winning? This calculator's break-even outbound volume.
Does a CDN, a same-region replica, or infrequent-access storage still beat the alternative on this workload? This calculator's linked follow-on pages, back on the calculator.

This calculator is deliberately provider-agnostic: it never fetches or stores a published price for AWS, another cloud provider, or anyone else. Every rate is one you type in, so it stays correct when a price sheet changes and works equally well for an AWS-to-AWS storage-class comparison, an AWS-versus-another-provider comparison, or a proposed price increase from your current vendor.

It needs no AWS account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off. Nothing you type is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or AWS's own Pricing Calculator?

Most people get more use out of both. AWS's own Pricing Calculator, at calculator.aws, is the authoritative source for what a specific AWS service configuration will cost, because it reads AWS's live published price list for the region and options you select. This page does not try to replace that lookup. What it adds is the decision AWS's tool is not built for: comparing two price sheets you already have — AWS against another provider, one storage class against another, or last year's rate against a new quote — on the same storage-plus-request-plus-egress workload, with the outbound-transfer volume where the cheaper-storage option stops being cheaper.

Is this page affiliated with Amazon Web Services?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Amazon.com, Inc. or its affiliates. AWS, Amazon S3, and AWS Pricing Calculator are trademarks of Amazon.com, Inc. or its affiliates, named here only to describe what this calculator is for.

Open the Cloud Egress Cost Calculator to run the comparison on your own rates.

vs-azure-pricing-calculator.html.text:
← Cloud egress cost calculator

This calculator vs. the Azure Pricing Calculator

Microsoft publishes its own free cost-estimation tool, the Azure Pricing Calculator, at azure.microsoft.com/pricing/calculator, documented at learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cost-management-billing/costs/pricing-calculator. Microsoft's own description there:

“The Azure pricing calculator helps you turn anticipated usage into an estimated cost, which makes it easier to plan and budget for your Azure usage. … When you log in, the calculator also provides a cost estimate for your Azure consumption with your negotiated or discounted prices.”

That makes it the right tool for one job: what a configuration of Azure products would cost on Microsoft's own schedule, and, once you sign in, on your own negotiated rate. It prices Azure services against Azure's numbers, which is something no third-party page, this one included, can claim to do. This site does not publish, cache, or endorse any provider's prices — it asks you to paste the rates from the price sheet or quote in front of you. Microsoft's own documentation is explicit that the figures it walks through are illustrative, not a quote:

“Prices shown in this article are examples to help you understand how the calculator works. They aren't actual prices.”

So if the question is an Azure number, open Microsoft's calculator; this page says so plainly. What it does not do is the thing this tool exists for — putting a second provider's sheet next to the first one on the same workload, which is the shape of an actual migration decision.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What would this storage account and this outbound volume cost on Azure? Microsoft's own Pricing Calculator — it prices Azure products on Microsoft's schedule, and your own negotiated rate once you sign in.
Provider A quoted me one sheet and provider B another. Which is cheaper on my stored GB, requests, and outbound transfer? This calculator — both sheets on one screen, from the rates you enter.
At what outbound volume does the cheaper storage rate stop being cheaper? This calculator's break-even line, solved from the two rate sets.
Does putting a CDN in front of the origin actually cut the bill at my cache-hit rate? This calculator's CDN vs origin-only page, including miss-fetch cost.
Is a second-region replica cheaper than paying a cross-region pull every month? This calculator's replica vs cross-region pull page.
Does an infrequent-access or archive class still win once restore fees land? This calculator's storage-class page.
I have a negotiated or discounted rate that only shows once I sign in. This calculator — every rate is a field you type, so a quoted rate works the same as a list price.

Getting the question right also matters more here than the arithmetic does. Azure, AWS, and Google Cloud each cut storage, request, and transfer-out charges into their own line items and their own free tiers, so a "per-GB egress rate" from one provider is not automatically the same line item as another provider's. This tool never assumes they match — it asks for one outbound rate per option and shows its working, rather than pretending a single number is comparable across two sheets you have not read.

Beyond the comparison itself, this tool needs no account, no Azure subscription, and no sign-in. It is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off. Nothing you type is uploaded anywhere, and the copyable decision summary deliberately carries the totals and the cheaper option without the rate sheet behind them, so pasting it into a migration ticket cannot leak a quote you are under NDA about.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or the Azure Pricing Calculator?

Most teams get more use out of both, because they answer different questions. The Azure Pricing Calculator turns anticipated Azure usage into an estimated cost on Microsoft's own schedule, so it is the right place to answer “what would this storage account and this outbound volume cost on Azure?” This page does not try to replace that, and it never publishes or endorses any provider's prices. What it adds is the comparison Microsoft's calculator is not built around: two providers' price sheets on one workload at the same time, the outbound-gigabyte volume where a cheaper storage rate stops being cheaper, and the CDN, replica, and storage-class calls that sit on top of that decision.

Why does this calculator make me type the rates in myself?

Because a rate this page had cached would be wrong the day a provider changed it, and you would have no way to tell. Every provider publishes its own current price sheet and its own estimator; those are the authoritative sources and this tool deliberately defers to them. Typing the rates also means the arithmetic works for a negotiated or discounted rate that only shows once you sign in to the provider's own calculator, and it means nothing you enter has to leave your browser.

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Microsoft Corporation. Microsoft, Azure, and Azure Pricing Calculator are trademarks of Microsoft Corporation, named here only to describe what this calculator is for and to point at the primary sources quoted on this page.

It prices Google's products against Google's numbers, which is something no third-party page, this one included, can claim to do. Should I use this calculator or the Google Cloud Pricing Calculator?

Most teams get more use out of both, because they answer different questions. The Google Cloud Pricing Calculator estimates the cost of Google Cloud products you add and configure, priced against Google's own schedule, so it is the right place to answer “what would this bucket and this outbound volume cost on Google Cloud?” This page does not try to replace that, and it never publishes or endorses any provider's prices. What it adds is the comparison Google's calculator is not built around: two providers' price sheets on one workload at the same time, the outbound-gigabyte volume where a cheaper storage rate stops being cheaper, and the CDN, replica, and storage-class calls that sit on top of that decision.

Why does this calculator make me type the rates in myself?

Because a rate this page had cached would be wrong the day a provider changed it, and you would have no way to tell. Every provider publishes its own current price sheet and its own estimator; those are the authoritative sources and this tool deliberately defers to them. Typing the rates also means the arithmetic works for a negotiated or committed-use rate that no public sheet lists, and it means nothing you enter has to leave your browser.
